titre: “Not Proven”: The Scottish Verdict Walter Scott Hated
accroche: In Scotland, a jury could acquit by saying “not guilty” or “not proven.” Walter Scott, in 1827, saw in the latter a bastard verdict. It disappeared in 2026.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Edinburgh, the High Court of Justiciary tries Mary Smith, accused of poisoning a young servant, Margaret Warden, with arsenic. The trial, which opens on February 5, 1827, resumes on February 19 with a new jury. On February 20, at 2 p.m., the jury returns a unanimous verdict: “not proven.” Walter Scott, who is also a lawyer, attends the hearing; in his journal, he writes of “that bastard verdict, Not proven.”

The peculiarity of the system is that it has not two outcomes but three. A Scottish jury, made up of fifteen people, could declare the accused guilty, not guilty, or not proven. The last two verdicts are acquittals: the accused walks free, with the same legal effects. The difference lies in the message. “Not guilty” says the jury believes the accused innocent; “not proven” says it suspects the accused, without having enough to convict. Scott, for his part, believed the accused guilty.

## A disputed origin

Where does this third verdict come from? An often-repeated version ties it to a trial in 1728, that of Carnegie of Finhaven, accused of killing the Earl of Strathmore without intending to. His advocate, Robert Dundas, is said to have persuaded the jury to reassert an “ancient right” to judge the whole case rather than merely declare the facts proven or not. But the history of the verdict remains debated, and the sources are surer about its critics than about its birth.

## A verdict without a definition

The criticism has been constant: “not proven” carries no legal definition, as the Scottish Justice Secretary, Angela Constance, put it in 2025, calling it a “widely misunderstood” verdict. It left the complainer, the freed accused, and the public to guess what the jury had meant.

The Scottish Parliament voted to abolish it in 2025. The law, which received royal assent on October 30, 2025, removes the verdict for all new trials from January 1, 2026. It also changes the majority: ten jurors out of fifteen will now be needed to convict, instead of a simple majority.

After three centuries, a verdict that expressed doubt is thus replaced by two verdicts that express none. Whether doubt itself will be easier to express remains to be seen.

repere.texte: On February 20, 1827, the High Court of Justiciary in Edinburgh tries Mary Smith for the murder of Margaret Warden; the jury unanimously returns a “not proven” verdict, which Walter Scott calls in his journal “that bastard verdict.”

carte.punch: Scotland: three possible verdicts, one of which Walter Scott judged “bastard.”
carte.idee: A Scottish jury of fifteen could say guilty, not guilty, or “not proven.” The last two are acquittals. Voted in 2025, the abolition of the third applies to all new trials since January 1, 2026.

quiz.question: Why was the Scottish “not proven” verdict criticized?
choix: It allowed the judge to convict the accused despite the jury's verdict
It acquitted the accused without the law saying what the jury meant
It required a second trial before a jury of twelve
It reduced the sentence without releasing the accused, creating a murky status
quiz.explication: “Not proven” is an acquittal like “not guilty,” but without a legal definition: no one knows what the jury meant. It permits neither conviction by the judge, nor a new trial, nor a reduced sentence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Since the 2025 law, how many jurors are needed to convict an accused in Scotland?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law moves the rule to ten jurors out of fifteen, instead of the simple majority, which was eight. Unanimity is therefore not required.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What legal effects do “not guilty” and “not proven” have for the accused?
choix: They free the accused with the same legal effects
“Not proven” requires a second trial before another jury
Only “not guilty” frees the accused; “not proven” keeps him in detention
Both sentence the accused to a symbolic penalty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Both verdicts are acquittals: the accused walks free, with the same legal effects. What distinguishes them is the message sent by the jury, not the sanction.
